text:
**For a typical full-size fridge, get a power station with about 1,500–2,000 Wh of battery and at least 1,300–1,500 W of surge.** That size runs the fridge for about 24 hours. A 1,000 Wh unit covers roughly 16–17 hours.

## The three numbers to check

1. **Running watts (continuous output).** A full-size fridge draws about 100–250 W while the compressor runs. Almost any 1,000 W-class station handles that. ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage))
2. **Startup surge.** This is the number that most often rules a station out. Estimates of the compressor's startup spike vary:
   - 900–1,200 W according to [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)
   - 1,300 W as the allowance used by [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)
   - 1,200–2,400 W for large or older fridges according to [BlackBox](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)

   Aim for at least 1,300 W of surge, and more for a big French-door model. The station also needs a **pure sine wave** inverter.
3. **Battery capacity (Wh).** The compressor runs only about a third of the time, so a typical fridge averages just 40–70 W.

## Working out your own number

1. Find the kWh/year figure on your fridge's yellow EnergyGuide label.
2. Divide by 8,760 and multiply by 1,000. That gives the average watts. For example, 362 kWh/yr works out to about 41 W.
3. Multiply by 24 hours and by the number of days.
4. Divide by 0.85 to allow for inverter losses, then multiply by 1.2 for headroom.

For a typical fridge, one day comes to about **1,400 Wh**, and two days to about **2,800 Wh**. ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator))

Warm kitchens, opening the door, and ice makers all push the number up. Keep the door shut during the outage.

## Options by size

**~1 kWh (most of a day, about 17 hours)**
- Jackery Explorer 1000 v2: 1,070 Wh, about $499
- Anker SOLIX C1000: 1,056 Wh, about $470
- Bluetti AC180: 1,152 Wh, 2,700 W peak

Runtimes and prices are compared at [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/) and [BlackBox](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage).

**~1.5 kWh (about a full day)**
- **Anker SOLIX F1500:** 1,536 Wh, 1,800 W output, 2,400 W surge, LiFePO4 battery, 5-year warranty. It was listed at $599.99 (down from $1,199.99) on Oct 22. ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator), which has a "See it at Anker SOLIX" link)

**~2 kWh (about 33 hours, with room for other devices)**
- **Anker SOLIX S2000:** 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W output, 3,000 W peak, $699.99 after coupon. Buy at [ankersolix.com](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator).
- **BLUETTI AC200L:** 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W output, expandable to 8 kWh. It costs $899, or $854.05 with code **AFF5OFF**, which Dealectric reported working on 10/21. That is an affiliate link. Buy at [dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) ([details](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l)).

Prices change, so confirm at checkout.

**Before an outage, test the station with your fridge.** HomeGridHQ notes that some manufacturers' advertised surge ratings apply only to simple resistive loads like heaters, not to motors like a compressor. A real test is the only sure way to know the station can start your fridge.
